html:
Dynamical Systems

A complete reading on discrete dynamical systems: a state space, a map sending each state to the next, iterated over and over — and the question of what happens in the long run. We start in one dimension — fixed and periodic points, stability, cobweb diagrams, bifurcations, the period-doubling route to chaos of the logistic map — then use topological conjugacy, symbolic dynamics and the tent map to turn "chaos" into a precise mathematical object; finally we extend to higher-dimensional linear systems and linearisation, and finish with rotations and expanding maps on the circle. Continuous-time systems (differential equations) are treated in the Ordinary Differential Equations document of this library.

Three questions run through the text:

  1. Where do orbits end up? Fixed points, periodic orbits, limit sets — where does the system "settle"?
  2. Is that endpoint stable? After a small perturbation of the initial state does the orbit return, stay close, or run away?
  3. Are two systems "the same"? If there is a deformation preserving the orbit structure (topological conjugacy), a hard system can be studied through a simple one.

One fact worth remembering at the outset: extremely simple maps can have extremely complicated behaviour. x\mapsto4x(1-x) is just a parabola, yet it is sensitive to initial conditions, has dense periodic points and orbits that sweep out the whole interval. Each chapter first says what question it answers and the intuition, then gives definitions, results and proof ideas, and finally works the simplest examples.

Prerequisites: calculus (mean value theorem, Taylor expansion), linear algebra (eigenvalues, Jordan form) and a little of the language of metric spaces and topology (open sets, compactness, density).

Contents

  1. Overview: What Dynamical Systems Study
  2. Basic Concepts of Discrete Systems
  3. Continuity and Interval Maps
  4. Stability of Fixed Points and Periodic Orbits
  5. One-Dimensional Bifurcations
  6. Topological Conjugacy and Structural Stability
  7. Periods, Interval Covering and Chaos
  8. Symbolic Dynamics and the Tent Map

  10. Higher-Dimensional Discrete Systems
  11. Dynamics on the Circle
  12. Properties of Typical Systems at a Glance
  13. Problem-Solving Methods

Notation

Symbol Meaning
f^n the n-fold composition of f, f^0=\mathrm{id} (not a power)
\mathcal O^+(x) forward orbit \{f^n(x):n\ge0\}
\operatorname{per}(p) least period of a periodic point p
\operatorname{Fix}(f^n) the set of x with f^n(x)=x (includes points whose period divides n)
\omega(x) the \omega-limit set
Sf the Schwarz derivative
\Sigma_2^+ the one-sided two-symbol space; \sigma the shift
DF(p) Jacobian matrix; f^{-1}(A) always means the set preimage
\{t\} the fractional part of t

0. Overview: What Dynamical Systems Study

A discrete autonomous dynamical system is a state space X with a self-map f:X\to X: x_{n+1}=f(x_n). Price adjustment in economics, generations of a population in ecology, root-finding iterations in numerical analysis and pseudo-random number generators in computing all have this form.

The study has three layers:

Layer Question Tools
local how do orbits behave near a fixed or periodic point? derivative tests, multipliers, linearisation
parameter how does the structure change abruptly as a parameter varies? bifurcation theory, period-doubling cascade
global topological and statistical properties on the whole space conjugacy, symbolic dynamics, chaos, ergodic theory

Linearisation is the local dictionary: near a fixed point a smooth map "looks like" its linearisation, so in higher dimensions everything reduces to where the eigenvalues sit relative to the unit circle. Symbolic coding is the global dictionary: encode orbits as 0/1 sequences, and a complicated map becomes the shift, whose chaotic properties can be read off directly.

1. Basic Concepts of Discrete Systems

Intuition. An orbit is the "time series" of states. Some orbits eventually repeat (periodic), some fall onto a periodic orbit (eventually periodic), some never repeat. First make these words precise.

1.1 States, evolution and iteration

x_{n+1}=f(x_n),\qquad x_n=f^n(x_0),\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0,

with f^0=\mathrm{id}_X and f^{n+1}=f\circ f^n. A non-autonomous system is x_{n+1}=f_n(x_n). The forward orbit is \mathcal O^+(x)=\{f^n(x):n\ge0\}. A two-sided orbit \{f^n(x):n\in\mathbb Z\} is defined uniformly only if f is invertible; a non-invertible map may have no preimage or several, and negative iterates are not single-valued.

Example: doubling mod 9. On X=\mathbb Z/9\mathbb Z let f(x)=2x\bmod9:

1\to2\to4\to8\to7\to5\to1,\qquad3\leftrightarrow6,\qquad0\to0.

f^n(x)=2^nx\bmod9, so f^n(x)=x is equivalent to 9\mid(2^n-1)x.

1.2 Fixed, periodic and eventually periodic points

  • fixed point: f(p)=p;
  • periodic point: f^n(p)=p for some n\ge1; the least period \operatorname{per}(p) is the smallest such n;
  • eventually periodic point: f^m(x) is periodic for some m\ge0; if x itself is not periodic it is strictly eventually periodic.

\operatorname{Fix}(f^n) and \operatorname{Per}_n(f)=\{\operatorname{per}=n\} differ: the former also contains points whose least period is a divisor of n.

Divisibility of periods: if \operatorname{per}(p)=r then f^n(p)=p\iff r\mid n. In particular f^m(p)=p=f^n(p)\Rightarrow f^{\gcd(m,n)}(p)=p. Proof: write n=qr+s, 0\le s<r; then p=f^n(p)=f^s(p) and minimality forces s=0.

A strictly eventually periodic point forces f to be non-injective: f^{m+r}(x)=f^m(x), and if f were injective we could cancel f^m to get f^r(x)=x, a contradiction.

1.3 Limit sets and invariant sets

\omega(x)=\{y:\exists n_k\to\infty,\ f^{n_k}(x)\to y\}.

If the orbit closure is compact, \omega(x) is non-empty and compact; if f is continuous, f(\omega(x))=\omega(x). A set with f(A)\subseteq A is forward invariant, one with f(A)=A is fully invariant (textbook conventions differ, so state which is used).

If f is continuous and the whole sequence f^n(x)\to p, then f(p)=\lim f^{n+1}(x)=p: a single-point limit of an orbit must be a fixed point. For a mere subsequential limit this fails.

2. Continuity and Interval Maps

Intuition. One dimension has a special advantage: intervals are connected, so the intermediate value theorem directly gives existence of fixed and periodic points.

2.1 Metric spaces and continuity

A metric d satisfies positivity, symmetry and the triangle inequality; open balls B(x,\varepsilon)=\{y:d(x,y)<\varepsilon\}. Common metrics: |x-y| on the reals; Euclidean, max and \ell^1 on \mathbb R^m; the discrete metric. The Euclidean distance needs its square root; the squared distance generally violates the triangle inequality. Dense: \overline A=X, equivalently A meets every non-empty open set.

Equivalent forms of continuity of f:X\to Y: (1) \varepsilon-\delta; (2) f(B(x,\delta))\subseteq B(f(x),\varepsilon); (3) preimages of open sets are open; (4) preimages of closed sets are closed; (5) x_n\to x\Rightarrow f(x_n)\to f(x). (Here f^{-1}(U) is the preimage set and f need not be invertible.)

2.2 The fixed point theorem on a closed interval

Theorem. A continuous f:[a,b]\to[a,b] has a fixed point.

Proof: let g(x)=f(x)-x; g(a)\ge0,\ g(b)\le0; apply the intermediate value theorem. A bounded closed interval is essential: f(x)=x+1 on \mathbb R has no fixed point.

Covering form: if f is continuous and f([a,b])\supseteq[a,b], there is also a fixed point (pick u,v with f(u)=a,\ f(v)=b, so g(u)\le0\le g(v)).

2.3 Monotone maps

The set E of subsequential limits of a bounded real sequence is non-empty and compact, with \limsup=\max E, \liminf=\min E (unbounded sequences need the extended reals). If x<f(x)<p on (p-\eta,p), orbits starting there increase monotonically and are bounded above; the limit is a fixed point, and equals p if the interval contains no other fixed point.

  • a continuous non-decreasing interval map has no periodic orbit of least period greater than 1;
  • a continuous non-increasing interval map has periods only 1 or 2 (since f^2 is non-decreasing); if f(a)=b,\ f(b)=a is a 2-cycle, f has a fixed point in (a,b).

3. Stability of Fixed Points and Periodic Orbits

Intuition. A fixed point is an "equilibrium"; stability asks whether the system returns after a small push. In one dimension the answer is determined almost entirely by one number — the modulus of the derivative f'(p).

3.1 Definitions

Let f be continuous with f(p)=p.

  • Lyapunov stable: \forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta\,\forall y\in B(p,\delta)\,\forall n\ge0:\ d(f^n(y),p)<\varepsilon;
  • unstable: the negation of the above;
  • locally attracting: there is \eta>0 such that every y\in B(p,\eta) has f^n(y)\to p;
  • asymptotically stable = stable + locally attracting;
  • semi-stable: on the real line, attracting from one side and repelling from the other (say which side); unstable in the two-sided sense.

Stable does not mean convergent: the origin of f(x)=-x is stable, yet non-zero points move on a 2-cycle.

3.2 Cobweb diagrams

Draw y=f(x) and y=x in the same axes. From x_0 go vertically to the curve, horizontally to the diagonal, and repeat. With g=f-x: g>0 means a step to the right and g<0 to the left; if f'<0 orbits alternate sides and should be analysed through f^2.

Example: for f(x)=ax at the origin: |a|<1 asymptotically stable; a=1 stable but not attracting; a=-1 stable but not attracting (non-zero points form 2-cycles); |a|>1 unstable.

3.3 The first-derivative test

Theorem. Let f\in C^1 near a fixed point p. If |f'(p)|<1, p is asymptotically stable; if |f'(p)|>1, unstable; if |f'(p)|=1, the test is inconclusive.

When |f'(p)|\ne1 the fixed point is called hyperbolic.

Attracting case: pick |f'(p)|<q<1. By continuity of f', |f'|\le q on a small neighbourhood, and by the mean value theorem |f(x)-p|\le q|x-p|; the neighbourhood is forward invariant and |f^n(x)-p|\le q^n|x-p|\to0. The same estimate gives Lyapunov stability.

Repelling case: pick 1<q<|f'(p)|; on a small neighbourhood |f(x)-p|\ge q|x-p|, so as long as the orbit remains there its distance grows at least like q^n and any non-zero perturbation must eventually leave. One cannot extend the local estimate beyond the neighbourhood and conclude divergence to infinity.

3.4 f'(p)=1: higher-order tests

Suppose f(p+u)-(p+u)=au^k+o(u^k) with k\ge2 minimal and a\ne0. Then f is increasing nearby, and the sign of f(x)-x decides:

k a Behaviour
odd <0 attracting on both sides, asymptotically stable
odd >0 repelling on both sides, unstable
even >0 attracting on the left, repelling on the right
even <0 attracting on the right, repelling on the left

If no derivative gives a first non-zero term (e.g. infinitely flat), analyse f(x)-x directly; "infinitely differentiable" alone proves nothing.

Example 1: f(x)=2-\cos2x-\dfrac1{1+x} has f(x)=x+x^2+x^3+O(x^4) ⟹ 0 attracts on the left and repels on the right.

Example 2: f(x)=(x+1)e^x-e^{2x}+1-\cos x+\sin x: f(0)=0,\ f'(0)=1,\ f''(0)=0,\ f'''(0)=-5, so f(x)-x=-\tfrac56x^3+O(x^4) and the origin is asymptotically stable.

3.5 f'(p)=-1 and the Schwarz derivative

With F=f^2 we have F'(p)=1 and (for f\in C^3)

F''(p)=0,\qquad F'''(p)=-2f'''(p)-3[f''(p)]^2.

The Schwarz derivative is Sf=\dfrac{f'''}{f'}-\dfrac32\Big(\dfrac{f''}{f'}\Big)^2. Since f'(p)=-1 we get F'''(p)=2Sf(p). Hence: Sf(p)<0 asymptotically stable; Sf(p)>0 unstable; Sf(p)=0 needs higher order.

Example: f(x)=e^x\cos x-e^{2x}+x^2 with f(0)=0,\ f'(0)=-1,\ f''(0)=-2,\ f'''(0)=-10. Sf(0)=10-6=4>0 and (f^2)'''(0)=8>0: the origin is unstable.

3.6 Multipliers of periodic orbits

If f is continuous and f(p)=p, then for every integer m\ge1, the stability, attractivity and asymptotic stability of p for f and for f^m are respectively equivalent. The key is to write times as n=km+r, 0\le r<m, and control the intermediate times by the finitely many continuous maps f^r — checking only the subsequence f^{km}(y) is not enough.

For an orbit of least period r, p_i=f^i(p_0), the multiplier

\mu=(f^r)'(p_0)=\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}f'(p_i)

does not depend on the starting point. |\mu|<1 is asymptotically stable, |\mu|>1 unstable, |\mu|=1 needs higher order. In a general metric space the stability of the orbit of x compares d(f^n(y),f^n(x)), different from comparing distance to a fixed point.

Example: f(x)=2-x^2. Fixed points 1,-2 with derivatives -2,4 — both unstable. f^2(x)-x=-(x^2+x-2)(x^2-x-1); removing the fixed points leaves the 2-cycle (1\pm\sqrt5)/2 with multiplier 4p_0p_1=-4 — unstable.

3.7 Root-finding iteration and Newton's method

To solve F(x)=0 build G(x)=x+cF(x); a root p is a fixed point of G with G'(p)=1+cF'(p), and choosing c with |1+cF'(p)|<1 gives local convergence. Newton's method G(x)=x-F(x)/F'(x) has G'(p)=0 at a simple root and converges locally quadratically (F sufficiently smooth, F'(p)\ne0; not valid where the denominator vanishes or for starts far from the root).

4. One-Dimensional Bifurcations

Intuition. As a parameter \lambda varies continuously, the number or stability of fixed and periodic points can jump — a bifurcation. A one-dimensional fixed point can lose hyperbolicity in only two ways: the multiplier crosses +1 (saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork) or -1 (period doubling).

4.1 Concept

A one-parameter family f_\lambda(x)=f(x,\lambda). A qualitative change in the number, stability or local type of periodic orbits as \lambda crosses \lambda_0 is a bifurcation. The candidate condition for a local bifurcation of a one-dimensional fixed point is f'_{\lambda_0}(p)=\pm1; the exact type also depends on non-degeneracy conditions.

4.2 Saddle-node

f_\lambda(x)=x+x^2-\lambda: fixed points solve x^2=\lambda. None for \lambda<0; a semi-stable 0 at \lambda=0; two points \pm\sqrt\lambda for \lambda>0. With f'_\lambda=1+2x the negative branch is stable (0<\lambda<1) and the positive branch unstable. In general put H(x,\lambda)=f_\lambda(x)-x; if H=H_x=0,\ H_{xx}\ne0,\ H_\lambda\ne0 we have a non-degenerate saddle-node.

4.3 Pitchfork

f_\mu(x)=(1+\mu)x-x^3: fixed points 0 and, for \mu>0, \pm\sqrt\mu. For \mu<0 the origin is stable; for \mu>0 it is unstable and two stable new branches appear — a supercritical pitchfork. In the alternative form f_\lambda(x)=x^3-\lambda x the fixed-point equation is x(x^2-(\lambda+1))=0, so the critical value is \lambda=-1, and for \lambda>-1 the origin is stable and the non-zero pair unstable; one cannot read the stability direction off the cubic term alone and transfer it to another normal form.

4.4 Transcritical

f_\lambda(x)=\lambda x-x^2: branches 0 and \lambda-1 with f'_\lambda(0)=\lambda, f'_\lambda(\lambda-1)=2-\lambda; at \lambda=1 the two branches exchange stability. (For the form x^2-\lambda x the critical value is \lambda=-1 with branches 0,\lambda+1.)

4.5 Period doubling

Take again f_\lambda(x)=\lambda x-x^2. The non-zero fixed point has multiplier 2-\lambda, crossing -1 at \lambda=3. After removing the fixed-point factor the 2-cycle points satisfy

x^2-(\lambda+1)x+(\lambda+1)=0,\qquad x_\pm=\frac{\lambda+1\pm\sqrt{(\lambda+1)(\lambda-3)}}2.

For \lambda slightly above 3 a genuine 2-cycle appears, with multiplier

\mu=(\lambda-2x_+)(\lambda-2x_-)=-\lambda^2+2\lambda+4.

The 2-cycle is stable for 3<\lambda<1+\sqrt6; at \lambda=1+\sqrt6, \mu=-1, the candidate for the next doubling. The discriminant also allows a 2-cycle for \lambda<-1, whose stability must be checked separately through the multiplier. For the logistic family L_\lambda(x)=\lambda x(1-x) the 2-cycle points are the above divided by \lambda (\lambda\ne0).

4.6 The period-doubling cascade and Feigenbaum's constant

For the main period-doubling cascade of the logistic family, let \lambda_n be the parameter at which the stable period changes from 2^{n-1} to 2^n. They accumulate near 3.56995 and the ratio of gaps tends to

\delta=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\lambda_n-\lambda_{n-1}}{\lambda_{n+1}-\lambda_n}\approx4.66920.

This is a universal phenomenon for smooth unimodal maps, not a property of arbitrary one-parameter systems. Beyond the accumulation point there remain periodic windows; not every parameter is "chaotic".

5. Topological Conjugacy and Structural Stability

Intuition. Two systems that "look different" may have the same dynamics. Topological conjugacy makes "the same" precise: a continuous change of coordinates with continuous inverse that carries orbits of one system term by term onto orbits of the other. Hard systems (logistic) can then be studied through simple ones (tent, shift).

5.1 Definitions

A homeomorphism h:X\to Y is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse. If

h\circ f=g\circ h,

then f and g are topologically conjugate, and h\circ f^n=g^n\circ h. If h is merely a continuous surjection it is a semi-conjugacy, which does not guarantee that distinct points or orbits correspond one to one.

Conjugacy preserves least periods, density of periodic points, topological transitivity and minimality. On compact metric spaces it also preserves sensitive dependence (h,h^{-1} are uniformly continuous); on non-compact spaces this cannot be assumed.

5.2 Linear stretches

f(x)=ax, g(x)=bx with a,b>1 or 0<a,b<1. Take

h(x)=\operatorname{sgn}(x)|x|^\alpha,\quad\alpha=\frac{\log b}{\log a}>0,\quad h(0)=0;

then h(ax)=bh(x). Writing x^\alpha directly may be undefined for negative x, hence the signed power.

5.3 Quadratic, logistic and tent maps

  • Q(x)=1-2x^2 on [-1,1] and L(y)=4y(1-y) on [0,1]: with h(x)=(1+x)/2, h(Q(x))=L(h(x))=1-x^2, so they are conjugate.
  • The tent map T(t)=2t\ (t\le\tfrac12),\ 2-2t\ (t\ge\tfrac12). Take H(t)=\sin^2(\pi t/2); H:[0,1]\to[0,1] is a homeomorphism and H\circ T=L\circ H. So the full tent map and the logistic map with \lambda=4 have the same topological dynamics.

5.4 Structural stability

Fix the state space and the class of maps. In the C^r topology, f is C^r structurally stable if every g in some neighbourhood of f is topologically conjugate to f. On a compact interval use \|f-g\|_{C^r}=\max_{0\le j\le r}\sup_x|f^{(j)}-g^{(j)}|; on non-compact spaces the topology or the admissible perturbations must be specified. Hyperbolic fixed points are the prototype of structural stability; bifurcation points (multiplier \pm1) are not.

6. Periods, Interval Covering and Chaos

Intuition. A continuous one-dimensional map with a single point of period 3 necessarily has points of every period — "period three implies chaos" (Li–Yorke). This is the rigidity that connectedness of the interval brings: a map that "stretches and folds back" must create huge numbers of periodic orbits.

6.1 The covering method

Let I,J be non-degenerate compact intervals and f continuous. If f(I)\supseteq J there is a compact subinterval I'\subseteq I with f(I')=J. If there is a covering chain

I_0\to I_1\to\cdots\to I_{n-1}\to I_0,\qquad f(I_j)\supseteq I_{j+1},

then taking subintervals step by step and applying the fixed point theorem gives p with f^n(p)=p and f^j(p)\in I_j. This only guarantees a period dividing n; to get least period exactly n one must use the positions of the intervals to exclude shorter periods.

6.2 Sharkovsky's theorem

Order the positive integers: first all odd integers greater than 1 ascending, then 2 times those, 4 times those, …, and finally the powers of 2 descending:

3\succ5\succ7\succ\cdots\succ2\cdot3\succ2\cdot5\succ\cdots\succ2^2\cdot3\succ\cdots\succ\cdots\succ2^k\succ\cdots\succ8\succ4\succ2\succ1.

Theorem (Sharkovsky). If a continuous map of an interval has a point of least period m and m\succ n, it has a point of least period n.

In particular a 3-cycle implies all periods. The structure of the argument for period 3: order the three points of the cycle, which gives two adjacent intervals; use the images of the endpoints to read off covering relations; build closed itineraries of the prescribed length; finally exclude smaller periods.

6.3 Devaney chaos

Let f:X\to X be continuous on a metric space X.

  • topologically transitive: for all non-empty open U,V there is n\ge0 with f^n(U)\cap V\ne\varnothing;
  • sensitive dependence on initial conditions: there is a uniform \delta>0 such that for every x and \varepsilon>0 there are y\in B(x,\varepsilon) and some n\ge0 with d(f^n(x),f^n(y))>\delta (n may depend on x,y; separation is not required at all times);
  • Devaney chaos: dense periodic points + transitivity + sensitive dependence. In the usual infinite metric spaces without isolated points, the first two conditions of a continuous map imply the third; finite spaces must be checked separately.

"Having all periods" and "being Devaney chaotic on the whole space" are not the same statement; discussion of chaos must name the state space or the invariant set to which it is restricted.

7. Symbolic Dynamics and the Tent Map

Intuition. Coarse-grain the orbit — record only whether each step lands in the left or right half — and the orbit becomes a string of 0s and 1s. A complicated map then corresponds to an extremely simple system: shift the sequence one place to the left. The chaotic properties of the shift are transparent, and with the coding the chaos of the tent map is rigorously proved.

7.1 Symbol spaces

\Sigma_2^+=\{s=(s_0,s_1,\ldots):s_i\in\{0,1\}\}. For s\ne t let N(s,t)=\min\{j:s_j\ne t_j\} and d(s,t)=2^{-N(s,t)}. It satisfies the stronger ultrametric inequality d(s,u)\le\max\{d(s,t),d(t,u)\}; convergence of sequences means that any fixed-length prefix is eventually constant.

A finite word defines a cylinder [a_0\cdots a_n]=\{s:s_0=a_0,\dots,s_n=a_n\}, which is open and closed and forms a base of the topology. \Sigma_2^+ is compact, perfect and totally disconnected: a Cantor space. The two-sided space \Sigma_2 is indexed by \mathbb Z; the q-symbol space uses symbols \{0,\dots,q-1\}.

7.2 The shift

The left shift \sigma(s_0s_1s_2\cdots)=s_1s_2s_3\cdots is continuous and surjective but not injective on the one-sided space; the two-sided shift is a homeomorphism. The one-sided full shift is:

  1. dense in periodic points: every cylinder contains the periodic sequence formed by repeating its finite word;
  2. topologically transitive: given two cylinders, concatenate their words; after a suitable shift one passes from the first into the second;
  3. sensitive: change one symbol after a long common prefix; after shifting to that place the distance is 1 (any fixed 0<\delta<1 works).

So the full shift is Devaney chaotic, and it has a dense orbit (e.g. concatenate all finite binary words in turn).

7.3 Itineraries of the tent map

Let I_0=[0,\tfrac12],\ I_1=[\tfrac12,1]. A finite itinerary I_{s_0\cdots s_n}=\bigcap_{j=0}^nT^{-j}(I_{s_j}) is a compact interval of length 2^{-(n+1)}; the nested intersection of an infinite sequence is a single point \pi(s). The map \pi:\Sigma_2^+\to[0,1] is continuous and surjective with

T\circ\pi=\pi\circ\sigma.

The key point: this is a semi-conjugacy, not a conjugacy. The critical point and its preimages can have non-unique codes; and a Cantor space is totally disconnected whereas an interval is connected, so the two cannot be homeomorphic.

7.4 Chaos of the tent map

T^n has 2^n full branches, each of length 2^{-n} and mapped onto [0,1].

  • any open interval contains a full branch interval of high enough order, which some iterate maps onto [0,1] ⟹ transitivity;
  • periodic sequences are mapped by \pi to periodic points; surjectivity and continuity ⟹ dense periodic points;
  • in any small neighbourhood of any point there are nearby points whose eventual image is 0 or 1; at the corresponding time at least one of the two endpoints is at distance at least 1/2 from the original orbit; take \delta=1/3 ⟹ sensitive dependence.

So T is Devaney chaotic. T^n(x)=x has exactly 2^n solutions, but that does not mean 2^n points of least period n: if P_d is the number of points of least period exactly d, then

2^n=\sum_{d\mid n}P_d.

7.5 Cantor invariant sets for separated branches

If two disjoint compact intervals I_0,I_1 carry monotone branches, each covering I_0\cup I_1, with uniformly contracting inverse branches, then

\Lambda=\bigcap_{n\ge0}f^{-n}(I_0\cup I_1)

is a Cantor-type forward-invariant set. Every infinite itinerary corresponds to exactly one point, and coding gives a genuine topological conjugacy between \sigma and f|_\Lambda. This differs from the full tent map: separation of branches and contraction are the key conditions for uniqueness.

7.6 Subshifts of finite type and topological Markov chains

For a q\times q 0-1 matrix A=(a_{ij}):

\Sigma_A^+=\{s:a_{s_i,s_{i+1}}=1\ \forall i\},\qquad\#\operatorname{Fix}(\sigma^n|_{\Sigma_A^+})=\operatorname{tr}(A^n).

The formula counts points whose period divides n; the trace equals \sum_j\lambda_j^n (with algebraic multiplicity, no diagonalisability needed). If some A^N has all entries strictly positive, A is primitive and the shift is topologically mixing; in the non-trivial case of an infinite symbol space, periodic points are dense and the shift is sensitive, hence chaotic. Single-point spaces such as A=[1] must be excluded.

8. The Odometer and Minimality

Intuition. Not every "complicated" system is chaotic. The binary odometer "adds 1 and carries"; every orbit visits the whole space, yet there is no sensitive dependence at all — the opposite extreme of chaos.

8.1 The odometer

On \Sigma_2^+ regard s_0 as the lowest digit. \alpha = "add 1 with carry": all 1s before the first 0 become 0, the first 0 becomes 1, the rest is unchanged; the all-1 sequence goes to the all-0 sequence. Example: \alpha(11010\cdots)=00110\cdots. The first k digits represent an integer mod 2^k, and repeated addition of 1 cycles through all 2^k prefixes, so every orbit is dense.

8.2 Minimal systems

A system is minimal if every forward orbit is dense; on compact metric spaces this is equivalent to having no non-empty proper closed forward-invariant subset. Minimality implies topological transitivity. An infinite minimal system has no periodic points: a periodic orbit would be a finite closed forward-invariant set and would have to be the whole space.

The odometer is a minimal homeomorphism preserving the position of the first differing digit, so

d(\alpha(s),\alpha(t))=d(s,t).

It is an isometry with no sensitive dependence, hence not Devaney chaotic. \alpha^2 keeps the lowest digit fixed, so [0] and [1] are each invariant; thus \alpha^2 is neither minimal nor transitive — transitivity and minimality need not survive taking iterates.

At the accumulation point of period doubling in the logistic family, under suitable infinite-renormalisation conditions, the restriction to a particular Cantor invariant set is related to the odometer; this requires extra theory, does not follow from convergence of the doubling parameters alone, and certainly does not make the whole interval system minimal.

9. Higher-Dimensional Discrete Systems

Intuition. One dimension's "|f'|<1" becomes "all eigenvalues have modulus below 1". The linear system x_{n+1}=Ax_n is completely solvable; a nonlinear system near a fixed point is linearised through its Jacobian.

9.1 Linear systems

x_n=A^nx_0. Fixed points satisfy (A-I)p=0; if 1 is not an eigenvalue the origin is the only one. If all |\lambda_j|\ne1 the matrix A is hyperbolic.

Moduli of eigenvalues Type of the origin
all <1 sink, asymptotically stable
all >1 source, unstable
some <1, some >1 saddle, unstable
some modulus =1 non-hyperbolic, needs further analysis

A complex pair a\pm bi in two dimensions corresponds to the real block \begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix}=r\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}, r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}: a rotation combined with scaling; r<1 a spiral sink, r>1 a spiral source. Example: A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/3) expands in one direction and contracts in the other: a saddle.

9.2 Coordinate changes and Jordan form

If A is diagonalisable, P^{-1}AP=D and with y=P^{-1}x we get y_{n+1}=Dy_n: the two linear systems are linearly conjugate. Non-diagonalisable matrices have Jordan blocks J=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda&1\\0&\lambda\end{pmatrix}, and for \lambda\ne0

J^n=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda^n&n\lambda^{n-1}\\0&\lambda^n\end{pmatrix}.

So eigenvalues on the unit circle must be examined together with their Jordan blocks: modulus 1 with a 1\times1 block can be stable, while a 2\times2 block gives linear growth.

9.3 Nonlinear systems and linearisation

Let F:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m be C^1 with F(p)=p, and u=x-p:

F(p+u)-p=DF(p)u+o(\|u\|).

All eigenvalues of modulus <1 ⟹ locally asymptotically stable; some of modulus >1 ⟹ unstable; eigenvalues on the unit circle and none outside generally need higher-order analysis. For local diffeomorphisms the Hartman–Grobman theorem gives local topological conjugacy to the linearisation near a hyperbolic fixed point (with hypotheses such as local invertibility stated; it cannot be applied unconditionally to arbitrary smooth self-maps).

Example: F(x,y)=(2x-y^2+3,\ x-y). Fixed points: x=2y, y^2=x+3, i.e. (-2,-1) and (6,3). DF=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2y\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.

  • at (-2,-1): \lambda^2-\lambda-4=0, \lambda=(1\pm\sqrt{17})/2, both of modulus above 1 ⟹ source;
  • at (6,3): \lambda^2-\lambda+4=0, \lambda=(1\pm i\sqrt{15})/2, both of modulus 2 ⟹ spiral source.

9.4 Recurrences as systems

For a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}^2-a_n let x_n=a_{n+1},\ y_n=a_n to get (x_{n+1},y_{n+1})=(x_n^2-y_n,\ x_n), then find fixed points, compute the Jacobian and analyse the eigenvalues. Keep the order of the state variables consistent throughout.

10. Dynamics on the Circle

Intuition. The circle is an interval "with no end": walk to the end and you are back at the start. Two typical systems live on the circle — rotations (isometric, predictable, minimal) and expanding maps (stretching, chaotic) — the two extremes of dynamics; ergodic theory upgrades "dense orbits" to "time average equals space average".

10.1 The circle and rotations

S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z with distance d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,1-|x-y|\}. The rotation R_\alpha(x)=x+\alpha\bmod1 has R_\alpha^n(x)=x+n\alpha\bmod1 and preserves distance.

  • \alpha=p/q in lowest terms: every point has least period q;
  • \alpha irrational: no periodic points, every orbit dense — minimal but without sensitive dependence.

Density of irrational-rotation orbits: the pigeonhole principle gives arbitrarily small non-zero rotation steps, which then approximate any arc.

10.2 Measure and ergodicity

A rotation preserves normalised length measure m: m(R_\alpha^{-1}A)=m(A). A measure-preserving transformation is ergodic if every (mod-zero) invariant measurable set has measure 0 or 1. The irrational rotation is ergodic, and uniquely ergodic, for length measure: for any continuous \varphi and every x,

\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\varphi(R_\alpha^k(x))\longrightarrow\int_{S^1}\varphi\,dm.

For a general ergodic system, equality of time and space averages is usually guaranteed only almost everywhere, not at every point.

Application: the leading digit of 2^n. Since \log_{10}2 is irrational, \{n\log_{10}2\} is equidistributed in [0,1). The leading digit is d exactly when it falls in an arc of length \log_{10}(1+1/d), so the frequency is

\log_{10}\Big(1+\frac1d\Big).

Density of an orbit only guarantees entering every arc; computing frequencies needs equidistribution.

10.3 Expanding maps of the circle

E_m(x)=mx\bmod1, integer m\ge2, E_m^n(x)=m^nx\bmod1. Orbits of rational points stay in finitely many residue classes of the same denominator, so every rational point is eventually periodic; a reduced fraction x=p/q is itself periodic iff \gcd(q,m)=1, otherwise there is a non-periodic initial segment. Moreover

E_m^n(x)=x\iff(m^n-1)x\in\mathbb Z,\qquad\#\operatorname{Fix}(E_m^n)=m^n-1.

E_m has dense periodic points, is transitive and sensitive: Devaney chaotic. The base-m coding relates it to the full shift, but rational points have two expansions, so one cannot directly claim a homeomorphic conjugacy with the symbol space on the whole circle.

10.4 A finite model: card shuffling

Shuffling can be seen as a finite version of the doubling map. But on a finite deck all orbits are periodic and a finite discrete space has no sensitive dependence in the usual sense; finite permutations must be kept apart from the continuous circle expansion. Example: the out-shuffle of eight cards, keeping the top and bottom cards fixed: (1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)\mapsto(1,5,2,6,3,7,4,8). Numbering formulas for other shuffles must be derived separately.

11. Properties of Typical Systems at a Glance

State spaces carry their usual topology; "dense periodic points" means the closure of the periodic points is the listed space; "all points stable" means every orbit is Lyapunov stable.

System and state space dense periodic points transitive sensitive minimal isometry all points stable
full tent map, [0,1] yes yes yes no no no
4x(1-x), [0,1] yes yes yes no no no
full one-sided shift, \Sigma_2^+ yes yes yes no no no
odometer \alpha no yes no yes yes yes
\alpha^2 no no no no yes yes
irrational circle rotation no yes no yes yes yes
rational circle rotation, whole circle yes no no no yes yes
mx\bmod1, m\ge2, circle yes yes yes no no no
1-x, [0,1] yes no no no yes yes
1-x, two-point space \{0,1\} yes yes no yes yes yes
2x, \mathbb R no no yes no no no

A finite periodic orbit is itself a minimal and transitive system without sensitive dependence — the state space cannot be omitted. Transitivity and minimality of f and of f^n are not generally equivalent.

12. Problem-Solving Methods

12.1 One-dimensional stability

  1. solve f(p)=p and check the point belongs to the prescribed state space;
  2. compute f'(p) and use the modulus test first;
  3. f'(p)=1: analyse the first non-zero term of f(x)-x, or its sign on both sides;
  4. f'(p)=-1: analyse f^2, possibly with the Schwarz derivative;
  5. periodic points: exclude shorter periods first, then compute the multiplier \prod f'(p_i);
  6. state clearly one-sided versus two-sided, local versus global.

12.2 Bifurcations

Solve the fixed-point branches, find candidate parameters where the multiplier equals \pm1, and compare numbers and stability on either side. For period doubling solve f^2(x)=x and remove the fixed-point factor; do not mistake coincident roots for new cycles.

12.3 Topological properties

State the space and topology first, then check separately dense periodic points, transitivity, sensitivity, minimality and isometry. When transferring results by conjugacy, write down the conjugating map and verify it is a homeomorphism; finite spaces, non-compact spaces and semi-conjugacies each need their conditions checked.

12.4 Higher dimensions

Find all fixed points, compute the Jacobian at each, and classify by the position of the eigenvalues relative to the unit circle. When an eigenvalue lies on the unit circle stop applying the hyperbolic test and turn to higher-order terms or special methods.

Common pitfalls:

  1. f^n is composition, not a power;
  2. stable ≠ asymptotically stable ≠ convergent;
  3. the number of points of \operatorname{Fix}(f^n) ≠ the number of points of least period n;
  4. between the tent map and the shift the relation is a semi-conjugacy, not a conjugacy;
  5. "having a 3-cycle" does not mean "Devaney chaotic on the whole space".
